title: Job 6:1–10
context: The speaker is Job, answering Eliphaz the Temanite, who has just urged him to see his suffering as the chastening of the Almighty (4:1–5:27; compare 5:17). Job does not argue doctrine here; he defends the weight of his complaint. His anguish, he says, would outweigh the sand of the seas, which is why his words have been rash (6:2–3). He feels the arrows of the Almighty within him (6:4), compares himself to an animal that cries out only when it lacks food (6:5), and describes the friends’ counsel, or perhaps his own condition, as tasteless and loathsome food (6:6–7); the precise sense of these images is uncertain, and translations differ. He then asks that God would crush him and cut him off, finding consolation that he has not denied the words of the Holy One (6:8–10). This is the language of lament, addressed toward God rather than acted on. The book later says that the friends did not speak rightly of God as Job did (42:7), while Job also confesses that he spoke of things he did not understand (42:3). Both traditions read this unit as honest lament, neither endorsed as doctrine nor condemned as unbelief.

verses.arminianNotes: “Then Job answered.” Arminian readers note that Job now replies to Eliphaz, who has urged him to accept his suffering as God’s correction. Job speaks for himself, and the book gives his voice full weight alongside the friends’ voices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the dialogue continues with Job’s reply, and they keep in view the narrator’s earlier verdict that Job had not sinned with his lips (2:10). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing a speech of honest lament from the one the book calls blameless (1:1).

verses.text: “Oh that my anguish were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances!
verses.arminianNotes: Job wishes his anguish could be weighed in the balances. Arminian readers hear a plea to be understood. Job feels that the friends have measured his words without measuring his pain, and he asks that his suffering be given its true weight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a sufferer longing for his grief to be recognized. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a reminder that words spoken in deep pain must be heard in light of that pain, and both commend patience toward those who lament.

verses.text: For now it would be heavier than the sand of the seas, therefore my words have been rash.
verses.arminianNotes: His calamity would be heavier than the sand of the seas, “therefore my words have been rash.” Arminian readers note Job’s candor: he admits that his words were rash and explains them by the weight of his suffering, without retracting his complaint.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the admission and see in it Job’s honesty before God and his friends. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as neither excusing everything Job says nor condemning him for speaking, and both see the honesty of lament as part of faithful speech.

verses.text: For the arrows of the Almighty are within me. My spirit drinks up their poison. The terrors of God set themselves in array against me.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the arrows of the Almighty are within me.” Arminian readers hear Job naming his experience honestly: he feels his suffering as coming from God. The book’s prologue shows a fuller picture than Job can see (1:12; 2:6), and they read his words as lament, not settled doctrine.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear honest anguish and recall that the prologue places all of Job’s trials under God’s permission and rule. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly and pastorally, as the cry of a sufferer, and the question of God’s relation to the evil agent in chapters 1–2 is treated at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass? Or does the ox low over his fodder?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether a wild donkey brays when it has grass, or an ox lows over its fodder. Arminian readers note the point: creatures cry out when something is wrong. Job’s complaint is not empty noise but the natural cry of real need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image as Job’s defense of the legitimacy of his lament. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an appeal to ordinary experience, reminding hearers that the cries of the suffering usually have a real cause.

verses.text: Can that which has no flavor be eaten without salt? Or is there any taste in the white of an egg?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether tasteless food can be eaten without salt, or whether there is taste in what is rendered “the white of an egg.” Arminian readers note that the exact sense of this phrase is uncertain. Job is saying that something offered to him is unpalatable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the uncertain wording and avoid pressing it. Some take the tasteless food to be the friends’ counsel, others Job’s own suffering. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse cautiously, as a vivid image of something Job cannot accept, without building conclusions on an obscure phrase.

verses.text: My soul refuses to touch them. They are as loathsome food to me.
verses.arminianNotes: “My soul refuses to touch them. They are as loathsome food to me.” Arminian readers note that the reference of “them” is not fully clear. Job is expressing revulsion at what he has been given to endure or to accept.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the precise reference loosely, while hearing the depth of Job’s distress. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s lament about something he finds unbearable, and both avoid resolving what the text leaves uncertain.

verses.text: “Oh that I might have my request, that God would grant the thing that I long for,
verses.arminianNotes: Job longs for God to grant his request. Arminian readers note that even in despair Job addresses his desire to God. He brings his longing into the relationship instead of turning away from God altogether, which shows faith expressed through lament.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job directing his request to God, the one he believes holds his life. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honest prayerlike speech from a sufferer, and both note that it prepares for the startling request in the next verse.

verses.text: even that it would please God to crush me; that he would let loose his hand, and cut me off!
verses.arminianNotes: Job’s request is that God would crush him and cut him off. Arminian readers hear the depth of despair, voiced to God rather than acted upon. They treat the words with pastoral care, recognizing that sufferers sometimes long for relief through death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear anguish and note that Job leaves his life in God’s hands rather than taking it into his own. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly and compassionately, neither endorsing the wish nor scolding Job for speaking it, and both affirm that such cries may be brought to God.

verses.text: Let it still be my consolation, yes, let me exult in pain that doesn’t spare, that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
verses.arminianNotes: Job’s consolation is that he has “not denied the words of the Holy One,” even in unsparing pain. Arminian readers note that Job still values his faithfulness. His integrity matters to him, and he takes comfort in having held to God’s words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job’s comfort in his fidelity and recall that the LORD himself affirmed Job’s integrity (2:3). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as evidence that Job’s lament is not unbelief, and both handle his wish for death and his confidence together with care.
